_comment: Java Interview Kit — quiz questions for chapters 5-8. Keyed by topic slug.

questions.prompt: Why can you not write 'new T()' inside a generic class?
options: Because generics are only allowed on interfaces
Because the JVM forbids reflection in generic code
Because T might not have a no-arg constructor
Because erasure removes the type argument, so there is no T at run time to instantiate
questions.explanation: The compiler checks generic types and then deletes the type arguments, replacing each parameter with its leftmost bound or Object. By run time there is no T to construct. The standard workarounds are to pass a Class<T> token and use reflection, or, more cleanly, to pass a Supplier<T> such as User::new.
questions.citation: How it works — everything erasure forbids

questions.prompt: What does new ArrayList<String>().getClass() == new ArrayList<Integer>().getClass() evaluate to?
options: true — after erasure both are plain ArrayList, sharing one Class object
false — each parameterisation gets its own Class
It does not compile
It depends on whether the lists contain elements
questions.explanation: There is exactly one Class object for ArrayList. This is the same fact that makes instanceof List<String> illegal and makes two methods differing only in type arguments a duplicate-signature error.
questions.citation: Code examples — what erasure forbids

questions.prompt: What is a bridge method?
options: A method generated by the JIT to inline across class boundaries
A synthetic method the compiler generates so erasure still works with polymorphism — for example a compareTo(Object) that casts and delegates to your compareTo(Employee)
A method that converts between primitives and wrappers
A default method that connects two interfaces
questions.explanation: Implementing Comparable<Employee> gives you compareTo(Employee), but the erased interface declares compareTo(Object) — a different signature, so dispatch would break. The compiler inserts a bridge that casts and delegates. It is visible in javap output and occasionally appears in stack traces.
questions.citation: Under the hood — bridge methods

questions.prompt: Why can you not add an Integer to a List<? extends Number>?
options: Because wildcards make a collection immutable
Because Number is abstract
Because the actual list might be a List<Double>, and the compiler cannot prove the write is safe for every type the wildcard could stand for
Because Integer is not a subtype of Number
questions.explanation: '? extends Number' means some unknown subtype. Reading is safe — everything coming out is at least a Number — but writing is not, because adding an Integer to what is really a List<Double> would corrupt it. Only null, a valid value of every reference type, may be written.
questions.citation: How it works — why each restriction exists

questions.prompt: In 'void copy(List<? super T> dst, List<? extends T> src)', why are the wildcards that way round?
options: They are interchangeable; either order compiles
extends is always used for the first parameter by convention
super allows reading and extends allows writing
PECS — src PRODUCES elements so it uses extends; dst CONSUMES them so it uses super
questions.explanation: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. The source only ever has elements read out of it, so extends gives a usable read type. The destination only ever has elements written into it, so super guarantees a T is a legal element whatever the actual type is. This is essentially Collections.copy.
questions.citation: Code examples — the canonical signature

questions.prompt: How does List<?> differ from a raw List?
options: List<?> is fully checked — you can read as Object but cannot add anything except null — while a raw List disables generic checking entirely, so unsafe adds compile silently
List<?> is immutable; raw List is mutable
A raw List cannot be iterated
They are the same thing with different syntax
questions.explanation: List<?> means a list of some specific but unknown type, and the compiler enforces that. A raw type opts out of generic checking altogether, which is why it is never the right choice. Always prefer List<?> when you do not care about the element type.
questions.citation: Code examples — unbounded wildcards and the raw-type trap

questions.prompt: What is wrong with the comparator (a, b) -> a.getAge() - b.getAge()?
options: It returns the wrong sign for equal values
Integer subtraction can overflow when the values straddle the int range, flipping the sign and reversing the order
It fails to compile without an explicit cast
Nothing — it is the idiomatic form
questions.explanation: With values near Integer.MAX_VALUE and negative numbers the subtraction wraps around and reports the opposite order. Integer.compare(a, b) is correct and just as readable. For doubles there is a second reason: Double.compare handles NaN and negative zero properly.
questions.citation: Code examples — the subtraction bug

questions.prompt: comparing(Employee::dept).thenComparing(Employee::salary).reversed() sorts by…
options: Department ascending, salary ascending
Department ascending, salary descending
Department DESCENDING and salary DESCENDING — reversed() flips the entire chain, not just the last key
Salary descending only
questions.explanation: reversed() applies to the whole comparator built so far. To reverse only one key, pass a comparator to that key: thenComparing(Employee::salary, Comparator.reverseOrder()). This is one of the most common comparator mistakes.
questions.citation: Code examples — modern Comparator composition

questions.prompt: What causes 'IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract'?
options: Comparing objects of different classes
Passing null to sort()
Sorting an immutable list
An inconsistent comparator — commonly one that never returns 0, or is not antisymmetric or transitive — detected by TimSort while merging
questions.explanation: TimSort merges assuming a consistent ordering; when its invariants become impossible it throws rather than silently corrupting the array. The check only fires on inputs large enough to trigger merging, typically 32 or more elements, which is why these bugs escape unit tests and appear in production.
questions.citation: How it works — the contract

questions.prompt: Which statement about the exception hierarchy is correct?
options: Unchecked means Error OR RuntimeException; everything else under Exception is checked
Unchecked means anything under Error; everything under Exception is checked
All exceptions are checked; only Errors are unchecked
RuntimeException is checked because it extends Exception
questions.explanation: The checked/unchecked line is not the Error/Exception line. RuntimeException sits under Exception but is unchecked, alongside Error. Everything else under Exception — IOException, SQLException, InterruptedException — is checked and subject to handle-or-declare.
questions.citation: The concept, simply — two branches

questions.prompt: Why is catching Throwable almost always a bug?
options: Because it is slower than catching Exception
Because it includes Error — OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError — so you continue running with the JVM in an unknown state
Because Throwable is abstract
Because the compiler forbids it
questions.explanation: An Error means something the application cannot fix. Catching it converts a clean crash into a process limping on with corrupted state. Even a top-level boundary handler should catch Exception, not Throwable.
questions.citation: Code examples — what not to catch

questions.prompt: Your production logs show NullPointerException with no stack trace at all. What is the most likely cause?
options: The logging framework is misconfigured
The exception was constructed with a null message
HotSpot's fast-throw optimisation: after the same implicit exception is thrown many times from one site, the JIT recompiles it to throw a pre-allocated instance with an empty trace
The stack was too deep to capture
questions.explanation: This is a real and widely misdiagnosed JVM behaviour. Disable it with -XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow to get traces back. Checking this before blaming the logging configuration saves a lot of time.
questions.citation: Under the hood — stack traces can disappear entirely

questions.prompt: Who enforces the checked-exception rule?
options: The security manager
Both javac and the bytecode verifier
The JVM, at class-load time
javac only — the JVM has no notion of checked exceptions, which is why the 'sneaky throws' trick works
questions.explanation: The throws clause is recorded in the class file for the compiler's benefit, but the JVM will let any exception propagate from anywhere. That is why a generics trick can throw a checked exception without declaring it, which is exactly what Lombok's @SneakyThrows does.
questions.citation: Under the hood — the JVM does not know about checked exceptions

questions.prompt: Can an overriding method declare a broader checked exception than the method it overrides?
options: No — it may narrow or drop checked exceptions but never broaden them, or code compiled against the parent would stop working
Yes, if the class is abstract
Only for unchecked exceptions
Yes, as long as it is still an Exception subclass
questions.explanation: This is Liskov substitution enforced by the language. A caller written against the parent type is not prepared to handle a new checked exception, so widening is a compile error. Unchecked exceptions are unrestricted.
questions.citation: How it works — interaction with inheritance

questions.prompt: Why can a lambda passed to Stream.map not throw IOException?
options: Because streams catch all exceptions internally
Because Function.apply does not declare a checked exception, and none of the standard functional interfaces do
Because IOException is unchecked in a lambda context
Because lambdas cannot throw any exceptions
questions.explanation: A lambda can only throw what its target functional interface declares. Since none of java.util.function declares checked exceptions, you must catch inside and wrap — which is exactly why the JDK ships UncheckedIOException — or define a throwing interface with an adapter.
questions.citation: How it works — they do not compose with lambdas

questions.prompt: int x = 1; try { return x; } finally { x = 2; }  What is returned?
options: A compile error
Undefined behaviour
1 — the return expression is evaluated and the value saved before finally runs
2 — finally runs last, so it wins
questions.explanation: The return value is computed and stored, then finally executes, then the saved value is returned. Assigning to x afterwards cannot change what was already captured. If the return were an object reference, MUTATING the object would be visible — but reassigning the variable still would not.
questions.citation: Code examples — the classic puzzle

questions.prompt: What happens if you return from inside a finally block while an exception is propagating?
options: Both the exception and the return value reach the caller
The exception is rethrown after the return
It is a compile error
The exception is DISCARDED entirely and the caller sees a normal return
questions.explanation: A return in finally overrides everything the try was doing, including an in-flight exception, which vanishes without a trace. The same applies to throwing from finally, which replaces the original exception. It is one of the few genuinely silent failure modes in Java, and linters flag it.
questions.citation: How it works — the two ways finally goes wrong

questions.prompt: When does a finally block NOT run?
options: When System.exit() is called, the JVM crashes, or the thread is killed
When the try block returns
When an exception is thrown but not caught
When a break or continue exits the try
questions.explanation: finally runs on every normal path out of the try — normal completion, caught exceptions, propagating exceptions, and return, break or continue. The only exceptions are cases where the process is going away regardless.
questions.citation: How it works — when finally does not run

questions.prompt: In what order are resources declared in a try-with-resources statement closed?
options: Alphabetically by variable name
Reverse order of declaration — last opened, first closed
Declaration order
Unspecified
questions.explanation: Reverse order is correct for wrapping: a BufferedReader declared after a FileReader must close first, and a JDBC ResultSet must close before its Statement and Connection.
questions.citation: How it works — three guarantees

questions.prompt: The try body throws and close() also throws. Which exception reaches the caller?
options: Only the first one thrown, with the other discarded
The one from close(), because it happened last
The one from the body — close()'s is attached to it as a suppressed exception, retrievable with getSuppressed()
Both are wrapped in a new CompositeException
questions.explanation: This is the main reason the construct exists. In a hand-written finally, an exception from close() REPLACES the body's exception, destroying the real diagnosis. Suppression preserves both, and stack traces print the suppressed one under its own heading.
questions.citation: How it works — the body's exception wins

questions.prompt: Which of these must be closed in a try-with-resources, despite looking like an ordinary stream?
options: list.stream()
IntStream.range(0, 10)
Stream.of("a", "b")
Files.lines(path) — it is backed by an open file handle
questions.explanation: Files.lines and Files.walk return AutoCloseable streams holding a file descriptor. Because almost no other stream needs closing, people use them like ordinary streams and leak descriptors until GC, which shows up on a busy server as 'too many open files'.
questions.citation: Code examples — real-world shape and a caveat

questions.prompt: When is creating a custom exception class justified?
options: When callers need to catch this failure specifically — to handle it differently, map it to a status code, or retry only this case
Whenever the message would be longer than one line
Only for checked exceptions
For every distinct failure in the application
questions.explanation: If nobody will ever catch it by type, a standard exception with a precise message is better — a class per failure mode adds vocabulary the codebase has to carry for no benefit. The JDK's standard types cover most validation cases already.
questions.citation: The concept, simply — when it is worth creating one

questions.prompt: Which is the most important constructor to provide on a custom exception?
options: One taking a numeric error code
One taking (String message, Throwable cause), so wrapping never loses the root cause
A copy constructor
A no-arg constructor
questions.explanation: Without a cause constructor, the first person who wraps another exception in yours loses the original stack trace — and the trace then points at your wrapper instead of the connection timeout that actually failed. It is the difference between a five-minute diagnosis and an afternoon.
questions.citation: How it works — four properties of a well-formed exception

questions.prompt: A lookup that legitimately misses about half the time. Exception or Optional?
options: An exception, because Optional cannot express failure
Always an exception — that is what they are for
Optional — an outcome that occurs on half of all calls is not exceptional, and a return value cannot be forgotten by the caller
Either; there is no practical difference
questions.explanation: Exceptions are for the exceptional, and constructing one walks the whole stack. A miss that happens routinely is a normal outcome and is better modelled as a return value the caller must handle. An exception is right when the absence indicates a broken invariant, such as a foreign key pointing at nothing.
questions.citation: Under the hood — a note on the modern alternative

questions.prompt: Is a lambda compiled into an anonymous inner class?
options: Yes, but only when it captures variables
No — lambdas are interpreted and never compiled
Yes — the compiler generates Outer$1.class for each one
No — the body becomes a private synthetic method and the use site becomes an invokedynamic instruction linked at run time by LambdaMetafactory
questions.explanation: Three consequences follow: no class file is generated per lambda, non-capturing lambdas are instantiated once and reused, and 'this' inside a lambda refers to the enclosing instance rather than a new object. The invokedynamic approach also lets the JDK improve the implementation without recompiling your code.
questions.citation: Under the hood — a lambda is not an anonymous class

questions.prompt: Why must a local variable captured by a lambda be final or effectively final?
options: Because the VALUE is copied into the lambda, and a lambda can outlive the stack frame — allowing reassignment would create two copies that silently disagree
Because lambdas run on a different thread
To prevent the lambda from being garbage collected
Because the compiler cannot infer the type otherwise
questions.explanation: Locals live on the stack, which may be gone by the time the lambda executes. Fields are exempt precisely because they live on the heap and are genuinely shared. The array-of-one workaround compiles but is not thread-safe and usually indicates you wanted a reduction.
questions.citation: How it works — effectively final capture

questions.prompt: What does 'this' refer to inside a lambda?
options: null
The enclosing instance — a lambda introduces no new scope for this, unlike an anonymous class
The functional interface being implemented
The lambda object itself
questions.explanation: In an anonymous class, this refers to the anonymous object and you need Outer.this to reach the enclosing one. In a lambda, this is simply the enclosing instance. It is the most common surprise when converting anonymous classes to lambdas.
questions.citation: How it works — this means the enclosing instance

questions.prompt: What does list.stream().map(this::save) do on its own?
options: Saves the first element only
Saves every element
Nothing at all — with no terminal operation the pipeline never executes, silently and without warning
Throws IllegalStateException
questions.explanation: Intermediate operations only record what to do; a terminal operation is what drives elements through the pipeline. A chain with no terminal is one of the most common stream bugs precisely because nothing complains.
questions.citation: Code examples — the silent no-op

questions.prompt: In stream().filter(f).map(m).findFirst() over four elements where the second matches, how many times does m run?
options: Four times, once per element
Three times
Twice
Once — elements flow one at a time through the whole pipeline and findFirst short-circuits, so elements 3 and 4 are never read
questions.explanation: The processing model is vertical, not stage-by-stage. Each element is pulled all the way through before the next starts, so a short-circuiting terminal stops as soon as it has an answer. A loop-shaped mental model would predict four filters and three maps.
questions.citation: Code examples — laziness made visible

questions.prompt: Why should peek() never contain logic?
options: Because it only sees elements the pipeline actually pulls, and the JDK is explicitly permitted to elide it — count() can skip the pipeline entirely when it can get the size from the source
Because it cannot access the element
Because it runs on a different thread
Because it is a terminal operation
questions.explanation: peek is documented for debugging. Anything that must happen belongs in a map or in the terminal operation, or it may simply never run.
questions.citation: Under the hood — peek is for debugging only

questions.prompt: Why does Collectors.toMap throw IllegalStateException?
options: Because the stream was empty
Duplicate keys — the two-argument form has no way to decide which value wins, so it refuses rather than silently dropping data
Because the values were not Comparable
Because the map exceeded its capacity
questions.explanation: Pass a third merge-function argument to say what happens on a collision. toMap also throws NullPointerException on a null value, which groupingBy does not — another reason to prefer grouping when values may be null.
questions.citation: Code examples — the toMap trap

questions.prompt: What is the difference between reduce and collect?
options: reduce is parallel and collect is sequential
They are equivalent; collect is just newer
reduce is for immutable folding into a single value; collect is for mutable accumulation into a container — using reduce with a mutable accumulator copies per element and breaks under parallelism
collect can only produce Lists
questions.explanation: Reducing into an ArrayList appears to work and is quadratic, because a correct reduce must not mutate its accumulator — and in parallel multiple threads would mutate the same container. Mutable accumulation is exactly what collect and its Collector contract exist for.
questions.citation: How it works — reduce versus collect

questions.prompt: Why prefer partitioningBy(predicate) over groupingBy on a boolean?
options: It is the only one that preserves encounter order
It allows more than two groups
partitioningBy is the only one that compiles with a predicate
It guarantees both true and false keys exist even when one side is empty, and uses a specialised two-entry map rather than a HashMap
questions.explanation: Grouping on a boolean can return a map missing one key entirely, which turns into a null check at every call site. Partitioning always yields both.
questions.citation: Under the hood — partitioningBy versus groupingBy

questions.prompt: Which thread pool do parallel streams use by default?
options: ForkJoinPool.commonPool() — shared by the entire JVM and sized to available cores minus one
The thread that created the stream, sequentially
A new pool per stream
The servlet container's request pool
questions.explanation: This is the single most important fact about parallel streams: the pool is a shared JVM-wide resource, so one slow pipeline starves every other user of it, including library code. Blocking I/O in a parallel stream is therefore an application-wide problem, not a local one.
questions.citation: The concept, simply — the critical detail

questions.prompt: Which source parallelises poorly?
options: IntStream.range(0, 1_000_000)
Stream.iterate — each element depends on the previous, so it cannot be split
An int[] array
An ArrayList
questions.explanation: Splitting is done by the source's Spliterator. Arrays, ArrayList and IntStream.range split by index in O(1) and produce balanced chunks. Stream.iterate is inherently sequential, and a LinkedList must be traversed to split — in both cases the overhead swamps any gain.
questions.citation: How it works — a cheaply splittable source

questions.prompt: list.parallelStream().forEach(results::add) where results is an ArrayList. What is wrong?
options: It will always throw ConcurrentModificationException
It works but is slower than a sequential forEach
ArrayList is not thread-safe, so this races — you get missing elements, nulls or an index exception, and it will pass a small test
Nothing — forEach is synchronised internally
questions.explanation: Collecting results by mutating a shared collection is the classic parallel-stream bug. The correct approach is collect or toList(), because collectors are written to build per-thread containers and combine them safely.
questions.citation: Code examples — shared mutable state

questions.prompt: What was Optional designed for?
options: Wrapping fields so they can be nullable
Passing optional method arguments
Replacing null everywhere in the codebase
A return type for methods that might not produce a result, so callers cannot silently ignore the empty case
questions.explanation: Brian Goetz has stated the intent directly: it is a return-type idiom, not a general Maybe type. That is why using it for fields and parameters goes against the design — and why it is not Serializable.
questions.citation: The concept, simply — what it was designed for

questions.prompt: What is the difference between orElse and orElseGet?
options: orElse takes a VALUE and always evaluates it, even when a value is present; orElseGet takes a supplier and only runs on the empty path
They are identical
orElseGet throws if the Optional is empty
orElse is for objects and orElseGet is for primitives
questions.explanation: For a constant either is fine. For anything expensive or with side effects — a database call, object construction — orElse silently does the work every time. The same reasoning is why orElseThrow takes a supplier: the exception and its stack trace are only built on the failure path.
questions.citation: Code examples — the eager-default trap

questions.prompt: Why should Optional not be used as a field type?
options: It always throws when serialised to JSON
It is not Serializable, it adds an allocation per instance, and it does not even stop the field itself being null
Fields cannot hold interfaces
It cannot be used with generics
questions.explanation: The non-serialisable point matters concretely for JPA entities, session objects and anything crossing a remote boundary. The idiomatic approach is to keep the field nullable and return Optional.ofNullable(...) from the accessor.
questions.citation: Code examples — where Optional does not belong

questions.prompt: What is the difference between calling start() and calling run() on a Thread?
options: run() creates the thread and start() schedules it
start() is deprecated in favour of run()
start() creates a new OS thread which then invokes run(); calling run() directly is an ordinary method call on the current thread with no concurrency at all
They are equivalent
questions.explanation: Calling run() directly compiles, executes the code sequentially, and gives no warning that you got it wrong. Calling start() twice throws IllegalThreadStateException, because a thread is single-use.
questions.citation: How it works — start versus run

questions.prompt: What is the decisive difference between Thread.sleep() and Object.wait()?
options: sleep releases locks and wait keeps them
sleep is more accurate
wait can only be used on collections
sleep KEEPS every lock it holds; wait RELEASES the monitor it was called on — which is why wait must be called inside synchronized
questions.explanation: wait must own the monitor in order to release it, hence the synchronized requirement and IllegalMonitorStateException otherwise. It also needs notify to resume, whereas sleep wakes on its own. sleep is static on Thread; wait is on Object.
questions.citation: How it works — sleep versus wait

questions.prompt: You catch InterruptedException and log it. What have you broken?
options: Catching it CLEARS the interrupt flag, so code above you that relies on the interrupt to stop work never sees it — cancellation and shutdown silently stop functioning
The thread terminates immediately
The exception is rethrown automatically at the next blocking call
Nothing, as long as you log it
questions.explanation: Either rethrow it, or restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt(). Swallowing it is one of the most damaging small mistakes in concurrent Java, because the failure is invisible until something needs to shut down.
questions.citation: Code examples — cooperative cancellation

questions.prompt: What TWO guarantees does synchronized provide?
options: Mutual exclusion and fairness
Mutual exclusion and VISIBILITY — releasing the monitor flushes writes and acquiring it invalidates cached values
Atomicity and immutability
Ordering and fairness
questions.explanation: People remember mutual exclusion and forget visibility, which is why they synchronise the writer and leave the reader unsynchronised — and then see stale values. Both sides need the lock to establish the happens-before edge.
questions.citation: How it works — two guarantees

questions.prompt: An instance method and a static method on the same class are both synchronized. Can they run at the same time?
options: No, synchronized always serialises the whole class
Only if the class is final
Yes — the instance method locks 'this' while the static method locks the Class object; they are different monitors
No, they share the class's lock
questions.explanation: They are separate locks, so if both touch the same shared state that is a race despite both being synchronized. It is a classic spot-the-bug question.
questions.citation: How it works — what object is locked

questions.prompt: Why prefer a private final lock object over synchronizing on 'this'?
options: Because 'this' cannot be used in static methods
It is faster
It allows more threads to enter
Because 'this' is public — any external code holding a reference can synchronize on your object and interfere with your locking, including deadlocking you
questions.explanation: A private final Object lock is unreachable from outside, so the locking protocol is genuinely yours. You also should never lock a String literal or a boxed value, since both are pooled and shared JVM-wide.
questions.citation: Code examples — the private lock object

questions.prompt: Does volatile make 'count++' thread-safe?
options: No — volatile gives visibility and ordering, not atomicity; increment is still read-modify-write and still races
Yes, but only for int and long
Only when combined with final
Yes — volatile makes the whole operation atomic
questions.explanation: volatile is the right tool for a value one thread writes and others read, where the new value does not depend on the old. As soon as the operation is read-modify-write you need an atomic class or a lock.
questions.citation: How it works — what volatile does not do

questions.prompt: A loop 'while (running) { }' on a non-volatile boolean may never exit. Why?
options: Because the JVM optimises empty loops away entirely
The write may sit in the writing core's cache, and the JIT — seeing nothing in the loop that could change the field — may hoist the read out of the loop entirely
Because boolean assignments are not atomic
Because the loop body is empty
questions.explanation: Two compounding reasons: cache visibility and compiler optimisation. Marking the field volatile forbids both. It is the canonical visibility bug, and it typically cannot be reproduced in a debugger because debugging inhibits the optimisation.
questions.citation: Code examples — the infinite loop

questions.prompt: Why does double-checked locking require the field to be volatile?
options: It does not — volatile is optional there
To make the null check atomic
Because 'instance = new Singleton()' is allocate, construct, assign — and the last two can be REORDERED, so another thread on the fast path could see a non-null reference to a half-constructed object
Because static fields are cached per thread
questions.explanation: volatile forbids that reordering. In practice the initialisation-on-demand holder idiom is better: it gets laziness and thread safety from the JVM's class-initialisation guarantee with no volatile and no double check. Before Java 5's memory model, DCL was broken even with volatile.
questions.citation: Code examples — double-checked locking

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of ReentrantLock compared with synchronized?
options: It cannot be used across methods
It is slower
It cannot be reentrant
Manual release — if unlock() is not in a finally block, any exception leaks the lock and every thread needing it afterwards blocks forever
questions.explanation: synchronized releases automatically even when the block throws. The idiom is lock(), then try immediately, with unlock() in finally — and nothing between lock() and try, or a failure there makes finally unlock a lock you never acquired.
questions.citation: How it works — the finally is not optional

questions.prompt: Why must await() always be called inside a while loop rather than an if?
options: Because await() can return without any signal — spurious wakeups are permitted and do happen — and because another thread may change the state before this one reacquires the lock
Because if statements cannot contain await()
To avoid deadlock
Because await() returns a boolean
questions.explanation: Both reasons require re-checking the condition after waking. The same rule applies to Object.wait(). Using if is one of the most common concurrency bugs in hand-written producer-consumer code.
questions.citation: Code examples — why the loop must be while

questions.prompt: What does Condition give you that wait/notify does not?
options: Better performance
Multiple wait-sets on one lock, so a bounded buffer can signal 'not full' and 'not empty' separately instead of waking every waiter
The ability to wait without holding a lock
Automatic deadlock detection
questions.explanation: An intrinsic monitor has a single wait-set, so notifyAll wakes everyone regardless of what they were waiting for, and notify can wake the wrong one and stall the system. Conditions let you wake exactly the right group.
questions.citation: How it works — Condition

questions.prompt: Which Coffman condition is the one you break in practice to prevent deadlock?
options: Mutual exclusion
No preemption
Circular wait — enforce a global lock ordering so a cycle cannot form
Hold and wait, by never holding more than one lock
questions.explanation: All four must hold simultaneously, but circular wait is the practical target: define a total order over locks, usually by a stable id, and always acquire in that order. Breaking hold-and-wait with tryLock and a timeout is the alternative when ordering is impractical.
questions.citation: The concept, simply — the four conditions

questions.prompt: Can the JVM recover from a deadlock?
options: Yes — it kills one thread as a victim, like a database
Yes, after a timeout
Only if the locks are ReentrantLocks
No — it can detect and report one in a thread dump, but there is no lock preemption and no rollback, so the threads stay stuck until the process restarts
questions.explanation: This is the contrast with a database, which detects deadlock, picks a victim transaction and rolls it back — which is why a database deadlock is retryable and a JVM deadlock is fatal. Prevention is the only real strategy.
questions.citation: Under the hood — the JVM detects but never resolves

questions.prompt: Why is calling a listener callback while holding a lock dangerous?
options: It is code you do not control — it may acquire another lock, call back into your class, or block on I/O, all while your lock is held
Because listeners always run on another thread
Because callbacks cannot be synchronized
It is not dangerous if the listener is final
questions.explanation: Alien code under a lock introduces ordering you cannot reason about. The fix is to copy the listener list inside the lock and invoke them outside it, so nothing you do not control ever runs while you hold a lock.
questions.citation: Code examples — the subtler deadlock

questions.prompt: In what order does ThreadPoolExecutor handle a submitted task?
options: It grows to maximumPoolSize first, then queues
Core threads first, then QUEUE the task, then grow toward maximumPoolSize only when the queue is full, then reject
It always queues first, then creates a thread per queued task
It rejects immediately if all core threads are busy
questions.explanation: Queueing before growing is the counter-intuitive part, and it has a major consequence: with an unbounded queue the pool never exceeds corePoolSize, so maximumPoolSize is dead code and the rejection handler never runs.
questions.citation: The concept, simply — the decision order

questions.prompt: What is dangerous about Executors.newFixedThreadPool in production?
options: It cannot be shut down
It creates too many threads
It uses an UNBOUNDED LinkedBlockingQueue, so a burst grows the queue until the heap is exhausted — and because the queue never fills, there is no backpressure signal at all
It never reuses threads
questions.explanation: newCachedThreadPool has the mirror problem: maximumPoolSize is Integer.MAX_VALUE, so it creates unbounded threads. Construct ThreadPoolExecutor directly with a bounded queue and an explicit rejection policy — CallerRunsPolicy gives natural backpressure.

questions.prompt: A task submitted with submit() throws an exception and nobody calls get(). What happens?
options: It propagates to the thread's uncaught exception handler
The executor shuts down
It is printed to stderr automatically
The exception is captured in the Future and never surfaces — it disappears entirely
questions.explanation: submit() captures the exception in the Future, so it only appears when someone calls get(). execute() propagates to the uncaught exception handler instead. The safest pattern is to catch inside the task so failures are always logged. A scheduled task that throws is worse — it is cancelled permanently.

questions.prompt: When should you use thenCompose rather than thenApply?
options: When the function itself returns another CompletableFuture — otherwise you get CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>>
When you need the result on a different thread
They are interchangeable
When the operation is synchronous
questions.explanation: It is exactly the map versus flatMap distinction from streams and Optional. Chaining an async call with thenApply produces a nested future you then have to unwrap.

questions.prompt: What does CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b, c) return?
options: The first result to complete
A CompletableFuture<Void> — it signals completion but does NOT collect results, so you still join each future afterwards
A blocking iterator over the results
A CompletableFuture<List<T>> containing all three results
questions.explanation: Joining each future is safe once allOf has completed, because they are all done by then. Not knowing this is a common stumble in the 'call three services in parallel' exercise.

questions.prompt: Why should you always pass an Executor to supplyAsync?
options: Because otherwise the future never completes
Because supplyAsync requires it
Because the default is the shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), sized for short CPU-bound work — blocking calls there starve every other user of that pool across the whole JVM
Because the default executor is single-threaded
questions.explanation: It is the same shared-pool problem as parallel streams. Passing your own executor is not a refinement; for anything blocking it is the correct default. Non-Async methods may also run on whichever thread completed the previous stage, or the caller.

questions.prompt: How does AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() work without a lock?
options: It disables interrupts during the update
It uses a ThreadLocal counter and sums on read
It synchronises internally on the AtomicInteger object
A retry loop around compare-and-swap: read the current value, compute the next, attempt an atomic swap, and start over if another thread got there first
questions.explanation: CAS is a single CPU instruction meaning 'if this location still holds the expected value, replace it'. No thread blocks — a loser simply re-reads and retries, which is fast at low contention and wasteful at high contention.

questions.prompt: Why does LongAdder outperform AtomicLong for a heavily-updated counter?
options: It keeps multiple padded cells so threads increment different memory locations, summing only on read — avoiding both CAS retry storms and false sharing on one cache line
It updates asynchronously on a background thread
It uses a lock instead of CAS
It stores the value as a double
questions.explanation: AtomicLong has every thread CASing one location, so under contention they retry constantly and invalidate each other's cache lines. LongAdder trades a slightly more expensive read for far cheaper writes — ideal for metrics, which are written constantly and read occasionally. Its sum() is approximate while writes are in flight.

questions.prompt: What is the ABA problem?
options: Two threads updating the same value simultaneously
A CAS succeeding because the value returned to its expected state after changing in between — the location looks untouched but the state moved underneath you
An atomic operation being interrupted mid-instruction
A deadlock between two atomic variables
questions.explanation: CAS only asks whether the value is still what you expected, not whether it changed and changed back. Harmless for a counter; genuinely dangerous for something like a lock-free stack where a node may have been recycled. AtomicStampedReference solves it by pairing the value with an ever-incrementing version.
